title: Rabbi Tachlifa of the West
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.
copyright: English translation and editorial notes © 2026 Joshua Waxman. All rights reserved.
paragraphs: Hyman suggests they called him so because in his time there was also an Amora in Babylonia named Rav Tachlifa, and he was from the Land of Israel, as Rashi explains on Bava Metzia 7a; therefore they called him “of the West.”

He still merited to be among the reciters of baraitot in Rabbi Yochanan’s academy, as in Menachot 14b: Rabbi Yochanan asked … Rav Tachlifa of the West taught him (in Dikdukei Soferim: bar Ma’arava). Hyman places him mainly before Rabbi Abbahu, noting that we always find “Rav Tachlifa of the West taught before Rabbi Abbahu,” as in Gittin 52b, Sotah 27a, Bava Kamma 33b, Bava Metzia 7a (“and Rabbi Abbahu showed him: and with an oath”), Bava Batra 77b and Sanhedrin 77b. They said in Berakhot 55a: “Rav Tachlifa of the West heard it from Rabbi Yochanan and went and said it before Rabbi Abbahu; he said to him: You teach it from there,” etc.
He used to go down to Babylonia, as in Ketubot 8a: “Rav Tachlifa of the West came to Babylonia and recited six long [blessings].”

Likewise in Eruvin 54b: “Rav Chisda said: The Torah is acquired only with mnemonic signs … Rav Tachlifa of the West heard it, went and said it before Rabbi Abbahu; he said to him: You teach it from there,” etc.

In Moed Katan 27a: “When Ravin came, a certain scholar said to him — and Rav Tachlifa of the West is his name — who was often in the tanners’ market”; in Nedarim 56a it reads “in the market of Tzilai.” Hyman explains the consistent title Rav Tachlifa by saying that he was not ordained.
In Moed Katan 9a we find “Tachlifa recited a baraita”; Hyman suggests that possibly he is Rav Tachlifa of the West.

notes.text: Here תנאים means reciters of baraitot in an Amoraic academy, not a claim that Tachlifa belonged to the Mishnah’s generation. גילדאי is the tanners’ market; צלעי remains the supplied variant Tzilai. The heading writes רבי while Hyman’s body explicitly argues for the consistent title רב; retain both with that discrepancy disclosed. Ordination and possible equivalence are Hyman’s claims.

The consulted Ketubot 8a directly has Tachlifa of the West coming to Babylonia and reciting six long blessings, followed by a ruling Hyman does not quote; that omitted conclusion is not inserted. Reciters of baraitot are not thereby dated to the Mishnah’s generation. Rabbi in the heading and Rav in Hyman’s argument remain distinct; his consistent-title, ordination and possible-equivalence arguments retain their force as his.
